title: The dream
hookLine: Ibrahim dreams he must sacrifice his son, the son says do as you're told, and Allah ransoms him with a great sacrifice

lines: OLD ENOUGH TO WALK WITH HIM.
A DREAM TOO HEAVY TO HOLD.
cards: The baby from the valley has grown. The Qur'an says he's old enough now to walk alongside his father, to work with him, the age when a son starts to be company. And Ibrahim has a dream.
In it, he is sacrificing his son. Some stories are too heavy to hold lightly, and this is one of them. For a prophet, a dream like that isn't just a dream.
What would you do with it? Ibrahim does something surprising. Before anything else, he tells his son, and asks him what he thinks.

teach.b: It's in Surah as-Saffat. Ibrahim says: my son, I have seen in a dream that I am sacrificing you, so look, what do you think? A father asking.
The son answers: my father, do what you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, among the patient. Then comes one of the most careful verses in the Qur'an.
When they had both submitted, and he had laid him down on his forehead. Both submitted. The Arabic is aslama, the same root as islam and Muslim: to surrender, to hand yourself over.
Father and son, together. And at that moment, a call: O Ibrahim, you have already fulfilled the dream. This was the clear test.
And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice. The knife never falls.
What was asked for was the willingness, and it was given. Which son? The Qur'an doesn't name him here.
Most Muslim scholars say Isma'il, partly because the good news of Ishaq comes a few verses later, as if he hadn't been born yet. Some early Muslim scholars said Ishaq.

Jewish and Christian scripture tell the story of Abraham and Isaac. Each tradition holds its own reading. Every year at Eid al-Adha, the festival of sacrifice, Muslims around the world remember this moment.
Many families sacrifice an animal and share the meat in thirds: for the household, for friends and relatives, and for people in need. The ransom became a meal.
And a story about a knife becomes, once a year, a story about feeding people.

how: At Eid al-Adha, during the days of Hajj, many Muslim families sacrifice a sheep, goat or cow in memory of Ibrahim's ransom and share the meat among the household, relatives and friends, and people in need.

ask him to wait for another dream.
games.why: he says do what you are commanded, you'll find me among the patient. then a call comes: the dream is fulfilled, and a great sacrifice ransoms him.

practice: Choose one small thing to give up for a day, nothing dramatic: your second coffee, dessert, scrolling at lunch, the last word in an argument, small enough that you'll do it and real enough that you'll notice.
Hold it in mind, say quietly, not today, and notice the little pull in you that resists; that pull is what the story is about. If you pray, you can offer the small thing up.

wordCard.voice: The dream. A father who asked, a son who agreed, and a ransom that meant the knife never fell.

orig.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 37:103: "they both submitted" — the same root as islam and Muslim.
